text: When your laptop loads a web page, it doesn't send the whole page as one giant transmission. It breaks the request and response into small, numbered pieces, sends each one across the network, and reassembles them in order on the other end. That lets a shared link carry many conversations fairly, and means a lost piece can be resent without resending everything.

Each piece gets a different name depending on which layer is handling it. Transport adds port numbers to make a segment. Network adds source and destination IP addresses to make a packet. Data Link adds source and destination MAC addresses to make a frame. Physical turns that into actual bits — electrical signals, light, or radio waves.
Each layer wraps the one above it in its own header, a process called encapsulation. The receiving device unwraps those headers one layer at a time, in reverse order, called de-encapsulation.

The OSI model gives IT professionals a shared seven-layer vocabulary for where a problem lives. Layer 7, Application, is the protocol the end-user app actually speaks, like HTTP. Layer 4, Transport, handles segments and reliability. Layer 3, Network, handles IP addressing and routing. Layer 1, Physical, is the literal cable, light, or radio signal.

This is why network troubleshooting goes bottom-up: confirm the cable is plugged in and the link light is on at Layer 1, before chasing an application error at Layer 7 — because nothing above a broken lower layer can possibly work, no matter how correctly it's configured.
Next lesson: the TCP/IP model, the four-layer model the real internet actually runs on, and exactly how it maps onto these same seven OSI layers.
